questions.prompt: When does an object's lifetime formally begin?
options: When storage of the proper size and alignment is obtained, regardless of any initialization.
When storage of the proper size and alignment is obtained AND its initialization is complete.
At the point of declaration, which is what makes the name visible to all the code that follows.
When the first member function is called on it, since that is the first observable use of it.
questions.explanation: Both conditions are required: bytes plus completed initialization. The 'storage obtained' answer is the tempting one because it is exactly half the rule — and it is the half that makes people believe `operator new` alone gives them an object. Declaration is a compile-time notion and has nothing to do with lifetime.

questions.prompt: You have `S* p = static_cast<S*>(::operator new(sizeof(S)));` and have not yet constructed anything. Which operation is legal?
options: Calling a non-virtual member function that touches no data members of the object at all.
Binding a `const S&` to `*p` so long as you never actually read through that reference.
Copying and comparing the pointer value, or reading the raw bytes through an `unsigned char*`.
Using `static_cast<Base*>(p)` to obtain a pointer to the base subobject of `S`.
questions.explanation: Outside the lifetime you may handle the pointer value and inspect bytes through `unsigned char*`/`std::byte*`, and nothing more. The non-virtual member call is the classic misconception — there is no 'it works because it doesn't touch members' carve-out; any member call is UB. Reference binding and base casts are equally forbidden.

questions.prompt: `struct C { const int id; }; C c{1}; c.~C(); new (&c) C{2}; int v = c.id;` What is the status of the read of `c.id`?
options: Well-defined and yields 2, because the new object exactly overlays the old storage of the same type.
UB — destroying an automatic object and reconstructing it in place is never permitted at all.
Well-defined but unspecified, so it yields either 1 or 2 depending on the optimizer's choices.
UB — `C` has a const member, so the old pointer is not transparently replaceable and may still read 1.
questions.explanation: Transparent replacement requires exact overlay, the same type, no const or reference non-static members, and not being a base subobject; the const `id` breaks it, so the compiler may have cached 1 and you need `std::launder(&c)->id`. The 'well-defined and yields 2' answer is the trap: the overlay and type conditions are met, but people forget the const-member condition, which is precisely why `optional::emplace` and `variant` launder internally.

questions.prompt: What does the standard's placement `operator new(std::size_t, void* p)` actually do?
options: It allocates from a per-thread arena seeded by `p`, then constructs the object at the result.
Nothing but return `p` — it is a non-replaceable no-op, and all the work is the constructor call.
It zero-fills the region of `sizeof(T)` bytes at `p` and then returns `p` to the caller.
It checks that `p` is suitably aligned for `T` and throws `std::bad_alloc` when it is not.
questions.explanation: The overload is defined by the standard, cannot be replaced, and simply returns its pointer argument; the observable effect of a placement-new expression comes entirely from running the constructor. The alignment-check answer is tempting because alignment really does matter here — but nothing checks it, which is why misalignment is silent UB rather than a thrown exception.

questions.prompt: Why is C++20's `constexpr std::vector` implemented with `std::construct_at` rather than plain placement new?
options: `construct_at` performs list-initialization, so it can aggregate-initialize elements that placement new cannot.
`construct_at` allocates the element storage itself, which placement new deliberately never does.
`construct_at` is the only form usable in a constant expression; plain placement new is not constexpr until C++26.
`construct_at` destroys any object already occupying the storage first, making the reuse well-defined.
questions.explanation: Constant evaluation forbids plain placement new until C++26, and `construct_at` is the sanctioned constexpr-friendly wrapper. The list-initialization answer inverts the truth: `construct_at` always performs direct-*non-list*-initialization, which is a known wart precisely because it cannot do brace or aggregate forms.

questions.prompt: `Base* b = new D1; b->~Base(); new (b) D2; b->f();` Why is the call UB, and what fixes it?
options: The compiler may have devirtualized based on the old vptr; `std::launder(b)->f()` discards that assumption.
The destructor call ended `b`'s storage as well as its lifetime; a fresh `operator new` is required.
`D1` and `D2` may differ in size, so the placement new overflowed; a larger buffer is what fixes it.
A strict-aliasing violation occurred by reusing a `Base*` for a `D2`; a `reinterpret_cast` fixes it.
questions.explanation: The vptr and any devirtualization decision are among the things a compiler may cache across in-place replacement, so the old pointer cannot be used and `launder` refreshes it. The aliasing answer is the popular misconception: `launder` does not legalize `reinterpret_cast` or fix aliasing violations, and a destructor call never releases storage.

questions.prompt: Bytes for a `MsgHeader` have just arrived in a buffer via `read()`, and no object was ever constructed there. Which facility is designed for this?
options: `std::launder(reinterpret_cast<MsgHeader*>(buf))`, which refreshes the pointer to the object there.
`std::construct_at(reinterpret_cast<MsgHeader*>(buf))`, which is the only zero-cost creation form.
`std::destroy_at(reinterpret_cast<MsgHeader*>(buf))`, which resets the region before you read it.
`std::start_lifetime_as<MsgHeader>(buf)`, which declares that the existing bytes are an object.
questions.explanation: `start_lifetime_as` (C++23) *makes* an implicit-lifetime object exist over foreign bytes; `launder` is the near-miss because it assumes an object is already alive at that address and only refreshes your pointer — with nothing ever constructed, there is nothing to launder. `construct_at` would run a constructor and overwrite the received bytes.

questions.prompt: At block scope, `int x;` versus `int y{};` — what is the difference?
options: Both are zero, since automatic storage is zero-filled on entry to the block by the platform ABI.
`x` is default-initialized and holds an indeterminate value; `y` is value-initialized and holds zero.
`x` is zero and `y` is indeterminate, because braces suppress the implicit zeroing of scalar types.
Both are indeterminate; empty braces only matter for class types that have a default constructor.
questions.explanation: Default-initialization of a scalar in automatic or dynamic storage leaves it indeterminate; value-initialization zeroes it. The 'both are zero' answer confuses block scope with namespace/static scope, where `int x;` really is zero via static initialization — the same syntax with a different answer depending on storage duration.

questions.prompt: Given `struct B { B() {} int x; };` and `struct C { C() = default; int x; };`, what do `B b{};` and `C c{};` leave in `x`?
options: Both are zero, because empty braces always mean value-initialization and value-initialization zeroes.
`b.x` is zero and `c.x` is indeterminate, because a written constructor body zero-fills before running.
`b.x` is indeterminate and `c.x` is zero, because `= default` on the first declaration is not user-provided.
Both are indeterminate, because each type has a user-declared constructor that suppresses the zeroing.
questions.explanation: Value-initialization zero-initializes first only when the default constructor is not user-provided; `B() {}` is user-provided and runs without touching `x`, while `C() = default;` on its first declaration is not. The 'both are zero' option is the natural but wrong generalization — 'value-init zeroes' holds for aggregates and scalars but not once a user-provided constructor intervenes. Moving the `= default` outside the class body flips `C` to indeterminate too.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `std::vector<int> v1(10, 5);` and `std::vector<int> v2{10, 5};`?
options: `v1` has two elements, 10 and 5; `v2` has ten elements equal to 5, since braces select the sizing constructor.
Both have ten elements equal to 5; the brace form merely additionally forbids narrowing conversions.
`v1` has ten elements all equal to 5; `v2` fails to compile because the two overloads are ambiguous.
`v1` has ten elements all equal to 5; `v2` has two elements, 10 and 5, via the `initializer_list` constructor.
questions.explanation: Brace-initialization prefers a viable `initializer_list` constructor over every other candidate, even a much better match, so `{10, 5}` is a two-element list. The 'both are ten fives' answer is what people expect from 'uniform' initialization — and it is exactly the reason containers with a size argument are the standing exception to the prefer-braces rule.

questions.prompt: On a hot path, `struct Buf { char data[65536]; }; Buf b{};` has what cost that `Buf b;` does not?
options: A 64 KB `memset`, because value-initializing the aggregate zeroes every byte of the member array.
A heap allocation, because value-initialization of a large aggregate is routed through `operator new`.
A guard-variable check, because value-initialized large locals are lowered to function-local statics.
A `memcpy` from a `.rodata` template, which is the only way to materialize a large aggregate value.
questions.explanation: Value-initializing a large aggregate emits a zero-fill, so the braces are a 64 KB `memset` that `Buf b;` skips entirely. The `.rodata` `memcpy` answer describes how a *non-zero* aggregate initializer is often lowered, which is why it sounds right — but zeroing needs no template. `Buf b;` is only safe if you genuinely write every field afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which of these initializations compiles cleanly?
options: `int b{3.5};` — braces convert the double to 3 exactly as parentheses do, with no diagnostic.
`char c{300};` — the constant fits after the implementation-defined wrap to a `char` value.
`int a(3.5);` — parenthesized initialization permits the narrowing conversion and truncates to 3.
`uint32_t d{-1};` — the conversion is well-defined modular arithmetic, so it is not narrowing.
questions.explanation: Only the parenthesized form allows the narrowing conversion; all three brace forms are ill-formed because narrowing is banned in list-initialization. The `uint32_t d{-1}` case is the most tempting: the conversion really is well-defined modular arithmetic at runtime, but 'well-defined' and 'non-narrowing' are different questions, and it is still an error.

questions.prompt: In which standard did aggregates first become permitted to have base classes, and how is the base initialized?
options: C++14, with the base initialized positionally like any other member: `Agg a{1, 2};` with no nesting.
C++17, with the base initialized by a nested brace group: `Agg a{{1}, 2};` for `struct Agg : Base`.
C++20, together with designated initializers, using `.Base = {1}` to name the base subobject.
C++11, provided the base is empty, in which case it contributes no initializer of its own at all.
questions.explanation: C++17 allowed aggregates to derive, with the base written as a leading nested brace group. C++14 is the near-miss because that is when a different aggregate restriction was lifted — NSDMIs became allowed — and C++20 is when designated initializers and parenthesized aggregate init arrived, but neither of those is the base-class change.

questions.prompt: For `struct Config { int port = 0; int backlog = 128; bool nodelay = false; };`, which C++20 designated initializer is valid?
options: `Config c{.nodelay = true, .port = 9000};` — designators may appear in any order the caller prefers.
`Config c{.port = 9000, .backlog.high = 4};` — nested designators name a subobject of a member.
`Config c{[1] = 256};` — array-style designators index the members of the aggregate positionally.
`Config c{.port = 9000, .nodelay = true};` — designators in declaration order with a skipped member.
questions.explanation: C++'s designated initializers are stricter than C's: initializers must appear in declaration order, though members may be skipped (they get their NSDMI or are value-initialized). The out-of-order form is the trap because it is perfectly legal C, as are nested and array designators — all three are C-only.

questions.prompt: What does `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(m);` do on a line by itself inside a function?
options: Creates an unnamed temporary guard that locks `m` and unlocks it at the end of the full-expression.
Declares a `lock_guard` named `m`, shadowing the mutex and providing no mutual exclusion at all.
Fails to compile, because `lock_guard` has no default constructor to satisfy such a declaration.
Locks `m` for the remainder of the enclosing scope, exactly as a named guard variable would do.
questions.explanation: Anything parseable as a declaration is a declaration, so the parentheses around `m` are redundant declarator parentheses and this declares a default-constructed guard named `m`. The 'temporary released immediately' reading is the common half-right answer — it correctly senses that nothing is protected, but the real mechanism is worse: no mutex is ever locked, and the mutex name is now shadowed.

questions.prompt: Which line actually declares and initializes an object rather than falling to the most vexing parse?
options: `Widget w();` — the empty parentheses read as a default-construction request for a local object.
`Widget w(Gadget());` — the inner `Gadget()` names a value and so forces an object declaration.
`Timer t(std::chrono::seconds(1));` — the argument cannot be parsed as a parameter declaration.
`std::scoped_lock(m);` — CTAD removes the template argument and with it the declaration reading.
questions.explanation: `std::chrono::seconds(1)` contains a value, `1`, that cannot be read as a parameter declaration, so the line really does declare and construct a `Timer`. The `scoped_lock` answer is the dangerous misconception: CTAD makes the trap *more* likely, not less, since dropping the template argument makes the accidental declaration shorter and more natural to write.

questions.prompt: `struct Holder { const std::string& s; Holder(const std::string& x) : s(x) {} }; Holder h{std::string("temp")};` What happens?
options: `h.s` is valid for `h`'s whole scope, because binding a temporary to a reference always extends its life.
`h.s` dangles: extension does not apply to reference members, so the temporary dies at the end of the full-expression.
`h.s` is valid until the constructor body ends, at which point the temporary is destroyed with the parameter.
The code fails to compile, because a temporary cannot bind to a reference member in a ctor-init-list.
questions.explanation: Extension applies to a temporary bound directly to a local reference, not to a reference *member* initialized in a ctor-init-list, so the temporary dies at the end of the full-expression that created `h` — and `h` outlives it. The 'valid until the constructor ends' answer is the sophisticated near-miss: it correctly senses the extension fails, but even that shorter window is not guaranteed here.

questions.prompt: `for (char c : get_vector_of_strings()[0]) { ... }` — what changed about this loop in C++23?
options: P2718 made the loop ill-formed, so the previously silent dangling is now a required compile-time error.
P2718 changed the range-initializer to be evaluated once per iteration, refreshing the temporary each pass.
P2718 extends all temporaries in the range-initializer to the loop's duration; before it, the vector died first.
P2718 requires the vector to be copied into the loop variable, which removes the reference into it entirely.
questions.explanation: The `auto&&` range variable extended only the subscript result's referent, not the vector temporary itself, so the vector was destroyed before the body ran; P2718 extends every temporary in the range-initializer to the loop's duration. The 'now ill-formed' answer is plausible because compilers do warn via `-Wdangling-gsl`, but the committee fixed the semantics rather than banning the code.

questions.prompt: A constructor acquires two raw resources in its body and the second acquisition throws. What happens?
options: The destructor runs and releases both resources, since the object's storage was already obtained.
Nothing leaks: the runtime tracks resources acquired in a constructor body and releases them on unwinding.
The first resource leaks and the members leak too, since no destructors run for a failed construction.
The first resource leaks: the object's destructor never runs, though fully-constructed members and bases are destroyed.
questions.explanation: A throwing constructor means the object's lifetime never began, so its destructor does not run — but every fully-constructed base and member subobject *is* destroyed in reverse order. That asymmetry is exactly why each resource should be its own RAII member rather than a raw handle acquired in the body; the 'the members leak too' answer gets the object right but wrongly extends the rule to members.

questions.prompt: The chapter names a non-obvious hot-path cost of RAII. Which is it?
options: Destructors are registered with `__cxa_atexit`, adding a table entry for every scoped object.
Unwinding tables for each scope must be paged in, so every guarded scope costs an extra cache miss.
A non-trivial destructor forces memory-passing at ABI boundaries and disables tail-call optimization.
The destructor call is dispatched through the vtable, which the compiler is then unable to devirtualize.
questions.explanation: The destructor body usually inlines to nothing, but its existence changes how the type crosses ABI boundaries and forces cleanup to run after a call returns, so a dispatch cannot become a `jmp`. The `__cxa_atexit` answer describes a real mechanism from a different section — it applies to namespace-scope statics, not automatic objects.

questions.prompt: `struct S { int a; int b; S(int x) : b(x), a(b) {} };` What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: the member-initializer list runs left to right, so `b` is set before `a` reads it.
`a` is initialized first, from an uninitialized `b`, because members initialize in declaration order.
`b` is initialized twice — once from `x` and again during `a`'s initialization — which is itself UB.
Reading another member inside a member-initializer is ill-formed regardless of the ordering here.
questions.explanation: Members are initialized in declaration order, so `a` runs first and reads a `b` that does not yet hold a value — `-Wreorder` exists for exactly this. The 'left to right' answer is the entire misconception the rule targets: the written order of the init-list is ignored, which is why writing it out of declaration order is a bug generator.

questions.prompt: A base-class constructor calls a virtual function that `Derived` overrides. Which override runs?
options: The derived one, because the object being built is ultimately of the most-derived type.
It is unspecified which runs, since the vptr's value mid-construction is implementation-defined.
The base's, because the dynamic type during construction is the class currently being constructed.
The derived one, unless the function is pure virtual in the base, in which case the base's runs.
questions.explanation: The vptr is set per construction stage, so a virtual call in a base constructor dispatches to the base's override; the rule exists because derived members do not exist yet. The 'the derived one, since the object is ultimately most-derived' answer is the intuition from finished objects and is the standard wrong answer. If the function is pure virtual in the base there is nothing to call — the program hits `__cxa_pure_virtual` and aborts.

questions.prompt: In what order are the parts of an object constructed?
options: Direct bases in declaration order, then virtual bases, then members in initializer-list order, then the body.
Members in declaration order, then direct bases in declaration order, then virtual bases, then the body.
Virtual bases, then direct bases in reverse declaration order, then members in declaration order, then the body.
Virtual bases first, then direct bases in declaration order, then members in declaration order, then the body.
questions.explanation: Virtual bases go first so they exist before any base that shares them, then direct bases and members each in declaration order, then the body; destruction is the exact reverse. The 'members in initializer-list order' answer is the most tempting because it embeds the widespread belief that the member-initializer list controls member order — it does not.

questions.prompt: What does `constinit` guarantee for `constinit std::atomic<uint64_t> g_seq{0};`?
options: It is constant-initialized in phase 1, so there is no dynamic initializer, no ordering hazard, no guard variable.
It is initialized on first use with thread-safe magic-static semantics, which removes any ordering hazard.
It is immutable after initialization, so the compiler may place it in `.rodata` and skip the dynamic phase.
It is initialized before every other global in the program, giving a deterministic cross-TU ordering.
questions.explanation: `constinit` asserts constant initialization — a compile error if the initializer is not a constant expression — so the object never participates in the dynamic phase at all. The 'initialized on first use with magic-static semantics' answer describes the *other* fix, a function-local static, which does solve ordering but at the cost of a guard-variable check on every call; `constinit` says nothing about mutability, unlike `constexpr`.

questions.prompt: A self-registering factory works when its .cpp is in the build, but registers nothing once the code moves into a static library. Why?
options: Static libraries strip `.init_array` entries at archive creation time, so no dynamic initializers survive.
Archive members are initialized after `main` begins, so registration happens too late to be observed.
Static libraries force all their globals to be constant-initialized, which skips the registering constructor.
The object file is never referenced, so the linker never pulls it from the archive and its initializer never runs.
questions.explanation: A linker takes an archive member only if something references a symbol in it, and a translation unit whose only purpose is a side-effecting static initializer is never pulled in. The fix is `--whole-archive` or an explicit reference from live code. The `.init_array` answer sounds mechanical and plausible, but that section is present and intact — it just never reaches the link.

questions.prompt: Given `struct Empty {}; struct WithMember { Empty e; int i; }; struct WithBase : Empty { int i; };` what are the sizes on a typical ABI?
options: Both are 4, because an empty class contributes nothing whether it appears as a member or as a base.
`WithMember` is 8 and `WithBase` is 4, because an empty base subobject may occupy zero bytes.
Both are 8, because every empty class needs a unique address and the alignment then forces padding.
`WithMember` is 4 and `WithBase` is 8, because a base subobject adds a vptr-sized table entry.
questions.explanation: An empty *object* must have `sizeof >= 1` so distinct objects have distinct addresses, forcing a byte plus padding for the member; a base subobject carries no such requirement, so EBO makes it free. 'Both are 4' is the tempting answer for anyone who knows EBO exists but applies it to members too — that is precisely what `[[no_unique_address]]` was added in C++20 to enable.

questions.prompt: `struct S { [[no_unique_address]] Empty a, b; int i; };` — why is `sizeof(S)` 8 rather than 4?
options: The attribute is a permission not a requirement, and compilers decline it when a class has several members.
The attribute applies only to the first declared member of a class, so `b` is laid out as an ordinary member.
`a` and `b` are distinct objects of the same type, so they need distinct addresses and cannot share offset 0.
The attribute never applies to members declared in a comma-separated list, so each needs its own declaration.
questions.explanation: Two objects of the same type must be distinguishable by address, so only one of the pair can vanish — wrapping one in a distinct tag type restores the optimization. The 'the attribute is a permission not a requirement' answer is half-true and therefore tempting: the attribute genuinely is only a permission, but that is not why it fails here; this is a hard constraint, the same one EBO has.

questions.prompt: `union U { int i; float f; }; U u; u.i = 1; float x = u.f;` What is the status of the read?
options: Well-defined in C++, since the common initial sequence rule covers members of the same size.
Well-defined in C++, because assigning to `u.i` began the lifetime of every member at offset zero.
Ill-formed in C++, since reading a non-active union member is a required compile-time diagnostic.
UB in C++, though GCC and Clang document type punning through a union as a supported extension.
questions.explanation: Only one member is active, and reading another is UB in C++ — the sole exception is the common initial sequence of standard-layout *structs* inside a union, which does not apply to two scalars. The 'the common initial sequence rule covers members of the same size' answer is the trap: people remember that a CIS rule exists and over-apply it. This read is legal in C, which is where the habit comes from.

questions.prompt: `union V { std::string s; std::vector<int> v; V() : s() {} ~V() {} };` — how do you switch the active member from `s` to `v`?
options: Assign `x.v = std::vector<int>{};` — assignment implicitly ends `s`'s lifetime and begins `v`'s, as for trivial members.
Call `x.s.~basic_string();` then `new (&x.v) std::vector<int>{};` — non-trivial members need explicit destroy and construct.
Call `x.~V();` then `new (&x) V{};` — the union's own destructor selects and destroys the active member for you.
Nothing special is needed — the compiler tracks the active member and inserts a destructor call at the assignment.
questions.explanation: Implicit activation by assignment works only for members of trivial type; for non-trivial ones you must destroy the old member and placement-new the new one, tracking which is active yourself. The assignment answer is the trap because that rule is real — it just does not extend to non-trivial types. The user-provided `~V() {}` exists precisely because the union cannot know which member to destroy.

questions.prompt: `struct Base { ~Base(); }; struct Derived : Base { std::vector<int> v; }; Base* p = new Derived; delete p;` What actually goes wrong?
options: UB, but harmless in practice: the derived destructor is skipped while the allocator still frees the block correctly.
Well-defined: the compiler emits a call to the correct destructor because the dynamic type is known at the `new` site.
A leak only: the standard still requires `operator delete` to receive the original pointer and the dynamic size.
UB: `Derived::~Derived` never runs so `v` leaks, and `operator delete` gets the base subobject's address and `sizeof(Base)`.
questions.explanation: Without a virtual destructor there is no deleting-destructor vtable slot, so the derived destructor is skipped and deallocation is driven by the static type — under multiple inheritance the base subobject's address is genuinely a different pointer, which corrupts the allocator rather than merely leaking. The 'UB, but harmless in practice' answer is the widespread 'it's only a leak' folklore, and sized deallocation makes it worse, not better.

questions.prompt: Why does `shared_ptr<Base> p = make_shared<Derived>()` destroy correctly without a virtual destructor, while `unique_ptr` does not?
options: `shared_ptr` stores the dynamic type in the control block and performs a `dynamic_cast` before destroying.
`shared_ptr` always allocates the object and control block together, so it can free by size rather than by type.
`shared_ptr` type-erases the deleter into the control block at construction; `unique_ptr`'s deleter is part of its type.
`shared_ptr` synthesizes a virtual destructor for `Base` at instantiation, which `unique_ptr` is not allowed to do.
questions.explanation: The control block captures a deleter matching the *constructing* type, so it destroys as `Derived` regardless of the pointer's static type; `unique_ptr<Base>`'s deleter is baked into its type and calls `~Base()`. The `dynamic_cast` answer is superficially plausible but would require `Base` to be polymorphic — the whole premise here is that it is not.

questions.prompt: Why did the committee standardize sized deallocation in C++14?
options: Size-class allocators otherwise look the size up from the pointer — a dependent load and likely cache miss per free.
Without the size, `operator delete` cannot know how many array elements it must destroy before releasing storage.
It lets `operator delete` verify the size against the allocation header and so diagnose heap corruption cheaply.
It was required to make over-aligned types work, since alignment can only be derived from the object's size.
questions.explanation: tcmalloc, jemalloc, and pool allocators must map a pointer back to its size class, which is a radix-tree walk or span-header read on the free path; passing the compiler-known `sizeof(T)` turns that into arithmetic. The alignment answer confuses this with aligned allocation, a separate C++17 extension; element counts are the array cookie's job, not the deallocation function's.
